utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Karnavas, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And before that, I have to remind you that you have used one-third of your time allocated to you. And reading from the transcript yesterday, we believe there's still room for you to improve your cross-examination. For instance, you asked the same question several times. We understand that you got a point in your question, but maybe you could put it directly to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, yesterday we left off when I asked you to look at the order that was prepared by your commander which you claim you have never seen and to look at the part where it says that you must treat the war prisoners under the Geneva Conventions. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then after that, you gave a lengthy speech about all orders would have that in it, and then you went on about the massacres that occurred after the fall of Srebrenica. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you would be so kind as to look at the order that was prepared by your commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, for the record, that's D17/1. And if the Madam Usher could also give him D16/1, which is the Drina Corps order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nikolic, from reading the order from the Drina Corps, reading the order that was prepared by your commander, is it not true that the initial battle plan attacking Srebrenica never envisaged the actual taking over of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, might I just take a look at this document to remind myself what the goal of the attack was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Might I ask you before you look at it, as you sit here today, after meeting with your lawyers for hundreds of hours with the Prosecution for days and days and days preparing over here, you don't know what the goal was when Srebrenica was attacked? Are we to believe that, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, that's not what I said. All I want to do is to take a look at the point in which the goal of the attack is defined at Srebrenica in this document that you have just offered me and asked me to take a look at. I didn't talk about the goal of the attack on Srebrenica as such. If you ask me, I'll tell you. But with your permission, may I take a look at the document and to see what -- as it relates to your question. I have found it, Mr. Karnavas. It is actually in point 4. And if that's what you're asking me about with respect to that particular goal, then I've found the actual stipulation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is with respect to the Bratunac Brigade order dated July 5, 1995? Is that what you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the order by the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So for the record, you're looking at D16/1 that has been marked for identification. Now, from reading that, is it not a fact that when Srebrenica was attacked, the goal was not envisaged for the actual takeover of Srebrenica; but rather, the shrinking of the enclave, that enclave and the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. And we have the objective here. I don't want to comment. What it says is what is written in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And that was your understanding at the time as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So before the attack on Srebrenica, you knew that Srebrenica would be attacked, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, sometime around the 10th of July, the order changed from above to actually go ahead and take Srebrenica because the Serb forces were advancing quite rapidly and quite successfully. Is that not true? Or are you not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I can't confirm when the decision was actually made. All I can do is to assume that the decision was made at the level of command, the command level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "the level of command," you're talking about the Drina Corps command, right? Or are you talking about the main staff command? Or both?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which, or rather who was included in the planning and decision-making process. But it's common knowledge in the army, one knows who makes the decisions on combat operations. But I really don't know the composition and level at which this decision was actually taken and who actually made the decision. I can just make an assessment myself, but I don't think that it is my place to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if you look at the order that was prepared by your commander, I would like to go over it in specific as to what was tasked by the commander of his brigade, of his battalion, and of you. Now, I'm referring to D17/1 that was marked for identification. It's the July 5, 1995. If you would look at -- if I could focus your attention on paragraph 4, and then if you could look at paragraph 5 as well, and there's several subparagraphs to 5, all the way to 5.6, so we can discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have taken a look at it, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we can go through it point by point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, point 4 or paragraph number 4 gives a general description, does it not, of what was decided by the brigade commander as to what would happen? Whereas paragraph 5 goes to the individual battalions and other units and tasks them specifically. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Point 4 defines the decision of the commander, that is to say, he says: "I decided..." et cetera, and then it states what he decided. Whereas point 5, from what we can see here, issues orders to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or rather, I apologise, it's not the tasks that are issued, it is that the tasks are defined of the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, if you look at 5.1, that refers to the 1st Battalion. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And 5.2 to the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 5.3 to the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 5.4 to the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 5.5 to the reconnaissance platoon?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And 5.6 as to which unit would be the reserve unit. And in this case, the military police platoon was designated as the reserve unit.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in reading the tasks that were defined, is it not a fact that other than the 3rd Battalion, the 1st, the 2nd, the 4th had primarily, if not essentially, defensive tasks and not offensive tasks?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're once again asking me, Mr. Karnavas, to comment an order which I haven't read in its entirety, which means I didn't use it. And you're once again asking me to comment on something that I'm not acquainted with. For me to be able to comment on this order, I should have to have the order with me and to take the time to analyse everything that went before, the tasks previously issued by the superior command, and to take a look at the order issued, or rather written by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. And after having done that, I would be able to make a judgement as to what each unit was tasked to do, whether it was primarily defensive, an attack, or whatever. So I don't wish to comment such an important document with just a cursory glance at it for a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. We can make that available for you to analyse. But from your answer, can I assume that this document was not reviewed by you, your lawyers, and the expert that you brought in from Belgrade who I understand is from the air force security sector, or that's where he was, when you were going over your preparation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karnavas, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That you have never -- that you have never reviewed this document with your expert as far as what your roles might have been during the time of the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is this: I did not have the opportunity or maybe I don't remember, but I don't think I had the opportunity of doing so, and I don't have the document because yesterday when I went back to the Detention Unit, I looked through the documents that I received from the Prosecutor. And I did not find this particular document among those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could be so kind as to go to paragraph 12 of this document, and in the English version, it says: "Reconnaissance command post" and I believe it should say "forward command post." Paragraph 12 titled "commanding and communication," would you please look at that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have looked at it, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would I be correct in stating that the forward command post in accordance to this order, with respect to that particular mission, that is, the attack on Srebrenica, for the Bratunac Brigade was Pribicevac as designated by your commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. On the basis of this document, it does say that the command post was there, forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during the attack on Srebrenica, were you aware of the fact that Pribicevac was designated as the forward command post for the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before the attack. During the attack, I did know that the command post was at Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When you say during, the attack as I understand it began on the 6th. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So prior to the 6th, say, the evening of the 5th, you were unaware that the commander had designated Pribicevac which incidentally is where the 3rd Battalion is located, right, you didn't know that that had been designated as the forward command post for the Bratunac Brigade for the Srebrenica attack?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, as to Pribicevac, I know what was there at Pribicevac, which means that I know that the 3rd infantry battalion was there, as well as the command of the 3rd infantry battalion, and the tactical group of Pribicevac, and its commander. And I know everything about it, in fact. But as I've already stated or rather I commented yesterday along these lines, for me to know what the commander had actually decided and amongst other things where the forward command post was actually situated, I would have to have received this order, a copy of this order, sent to me as the chief of the intelligence organ. And not only as the chief of the intelligence organ in person, but as a man who was in charge, as somebody who was in charge of the professional guidance of the military police platoon. And as far as I was able to see here from glancing at it, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade is issuing orders to the reconnaissance platoon. Let me remind you of what the rules of service define for the security organs. If I am that individual, I am the officer in charge and responsible for the reconnaissance platoon as well. And it would be normal for me to have received this order. And then we wouldn't have this discussion. I would have been fully acquainted of this all this, I would know what my task was and what the task of the units whom I was in charge of. Professionally speaking, I know what the forward command post was and I would know the tasks of the subordinate units. In a word, I would know everything. But I already said I did not receive this order, it was not addressed to me, to the body whose chief I was, and it was not duty-bound to investigate to see what the commander had actually decided and what orders he had given to the individuals and how he defined all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you through? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's a very comprehensive answer. Thank you. I'm going to try to narrow my questions. Maybe I'm asking too broad of questions. Okay. So based on your answer, you woke up on the 6th, on the morning of 6 July 1995, and somehow it was revealed to you that there was an attack planned for Srebrenica. And sometime thereafter, you learned that your commander had designated Pribicevac as his forward command post. That's the answer that you want us to believe. Right, based on your brief statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Object to the form of the question. That kind of attitude, that's not going to elicit any kind of reasonable response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do not need any lecture from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsels not speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's a way to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that the Prosecution has a right to make objections when you're doing your cross-examination, and you have to be very patient and polite to listen to what he's going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And you also have the full right to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, on the 6th of July, where were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to ask Your Honours to allow me to answer the previous question first because there were a lot of sweeping assessments made, qualifications and claims. Mr. Karnavas, I didn't wake up on the 6th, on that particular day, the 6th, and knowing nothing about what was going on and that I heard it for the first time. As for the attack on Srebrenica, as for my responsibilities and duties in that regard, both with respect to the intelligence sector and the security sector, as an officer, I was fully prepared for the tasks planned and operations planned. I should just like to -- their honours to hear what I have to say now. I did not avoid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Object to this, Your Honour. It's beyond the scope of the question. It's beyond the scope of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The witness hasn't finished his answer. We don't know whether it's beyond the scope of the question or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. In that event, with all due respect, Given that he's taking so much time to answer the questions, I may need additional time for my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear what the witness has to tell us first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, as I was saying, I was prepared. I knew an attack was to come. I knew what my duties were, my professional duties. So what you're saying is not correct, that I fell from the sky and moved around the brigade and the area of responsibility at random.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how could you be prepared for your professional duties if you didn't know and made no effort to find out what orders your commander had issued?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tasks of the intelligence organ are well-defined and common knowledge, Mr. Karnavas, except in cases where the commander in his decision does not issue separate tasks to be accomplished or if the commander by his decision defines special competencies and authorisations to the security organ and officer, the chief of the security organ, in fact. Or if the commanding officer writing out the order does not take away or has a special point defining that the security organ should not go ahead with those tasks for a particular period of time. But let me reiterate once again that I must receive all this in the form of an order, and then I act in conformity with that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So because you didn't receive an order formally from your commander, you didn't feel obliged that you had to act in any particular way, such as find out what might be in the order? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I really think, or rather, I do understand your question in part, and in part, I don't. And the fact that I should start asking around and roaming around, quite simply this could be taken incorrectly, that I was spying on the commander, that I was doing something behind his back, that I was trying to find out what was going on and find something out. So if the commander has anything to tell me or order me, he sends out an order. And the relationship there is quite clear. Any asking around on my part and questioning the order by the commander could give rise to suspicions on the part of the commander, and he would think that I was meddling and spying on the orders and decisions he had made and written, and I don't think that's the right way to go about things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at the last page, it shows who was delivered -- to whom these orders were delivered. And as you aptly pointed out yesterday, there were six copies, and your name is not on it, or your title. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But it does designate that the brigade chief of staff was provided with a copy, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, under the rules, is it not a fact that you, when it comes to your functions as intelligence, not security, because you're wearing two hats, and today we're focussing on security. So in your capacity as a security officer, do you not fall directly under the command of the chief of staff? Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He said security. I think he meant intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Intelligence. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you not come under the intelligence, or are you not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I am fully familiar with all the regulations of the law governing the internal relationships inside the brigade command. What I can say here is the following: I was the assistant -- I apologise -- the chief of the intelligence and security organ. As long as its part of the structure and as long as there are no amendments to this structure, you can't break it down like this. Momir Nikolic is an intelligence officer in the afternoon and a security officer in the morning. I am a single person and a single officer in charge of intelligence and security issues in the 1st Light Infantry Brigade and directly responsible to the direct commander. In brigades where these two duties are separate, where you have on the one hand chief of brigade security and then assistant chief of staff or intelligence on the other, the chief of intelligence in those brigades as I say is directly responsible to the commander. And the assistant chief for security affairs is directly linked and responsible to the chief of staff. The first level in terms of establishment and structure where these two duties are kept separate is the infantry brigade, such as, for example, the Zvornik infantry brigade where you had a special chief of security and a special chief of staff for intelligence affairs. So my answer to you would be the following: As chief of the intelligence and security affairs organ, I was directly linked to the commander. And I'm not part of the chief of staff's team. I am not responsible directly to the chief of staff. I am not subordinate to him directly. I do have a duty to forward intelligence, not only to the brigade commander but also to the chief of staff as well as other officers in other departments and services, in other branches, military branches, to the chief of artillery, the chief of engineers. My duty was to forward security-related information to them so they could make successful proposals to the commander as to how to use their artillery, their engineering equipment and so on and so forth. So this is the essence of what you have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could kindly look at Article 209 of the Brigade Rules. And I believe that is P83 for identification. If you could look at that, I believe it's the third paragraph, and tell me if it does not say "the chief of staff is directly in charge of intelligence support." Does it not say that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Can you please repeat which article you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 209. It's under the section of "intelligence support." It's the third paragraph. It's quite clear. And if anywhere in the rules here that you can find a distinction with respect to this issue of a brigade versus a light infantry brigade, I would like you to bring it to my attention because I haven't been able to find it myself.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I would like to ask you the following: 209, and which paragraph exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Number 3, it says -- in English, in English. I don't know what it says in Srpska. In English it says: "The chief of staff is directly in charge of intelligence support." I understand this was a light infantry brigade. You shared both positions. I appreciate that. But I'm just pointing out the rule itself. Am I reading it correctly? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're reading is correct. But this rule -- please, Mr. Karnavas, allow me to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This rule refers to the brigade, and you have the general rules defined here for infantry, to the motorised unit, for the mountain unit, the navy unit as well as for the light unit. This is defined here, and this is a general rule that applies to all these brigades. However, just a minute ago we spoke about the direct link, meaning to which officer in the brigade the intelligence officer would have been directly linked to. It is true that what it says here is that the chief of staff is directly in charge of intelligence support. This is beyond debate. But the command -- the relationship in command, the command links are different. The chain of command is different, and it goes exactly as I've just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Nikolic. But I guess I was moved, moved by your earlier answer that who could you go to -- you didn't want to appear as if you were snooping around your commander by going to the chief of staff and asking him about the order. And it shows here that he's the one that you're supposed to go to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. There's more motions and movements than it was a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Earlier you stated you did not wish to appear as if you were going around your commander, spying on him, trying to find out what might this order be on the largest attack the VRS had going during that particular year, where all these units are mobilised. And it shows right here that you could have very easily and very legally gone to the chief of staff had you wished to do so.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Karnavas, again, you're insinuating that I actually said something that I didn't say. I never referred to the chief of staff previously or going straight to him in order to spy on my commander. I never said a single word about this or did anything like that. I said it would have been inappropriate for me to go snooping around the command asking questions about the kind of decision the commander had made in relation to such an important attack, the attack on Srebrenica. That's what I said. I still believe this would have been extremely inappropriate, and this is just not done. Can you please ask me a direct question, straightforward question. I've explained to you the nature of link, direct link to the brigade commander and not to the chief of the staff. I've explained about the establishment or structure that was changed later on, and when it changed the relationship also changed. The chief of intelligence was directly linked to the chief of staff, but also remained in touch with the commander. If there's anything else that you want to know, please ask. But as I said yesterday, the brigade rules, in addition to broad, general regulations on intelligence and security affairs, do not fully define, but rather only in a very general way these two issues. And in my work, I did not use the brigade rules. I used the rules which apply to my area of work. But I am in part familiar with these rules. I have read them. I am, however, no expert on these rules, and it is not for me to interpret them or what they define.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Shall I take it we should go to your rules? That would make you more comfortable? To see what your defined tasks were in this particular situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to continue objecting. But we're not having questions, these comments are going to go on endlessly. I don't understand the relevance frankly. And these have been asked and answered. He's not putting his issue to the witness. It's going nowhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, I don't think there's any need for you to add so many words. If you have a point, just put it directly to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After an order is issued such as this one, is it not a fact, Mr. Nikolic, that you are to prepare an intelligence support order along with a plan that's attached to that order? Is that not your function under the intelligence support manual that you just referred to as what you used?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I must ask you, Mr. Karnavas, you've just asked me three questions in one. Please, ask me a clear-cut question. Let's go step by step. The first question you asked is what I was supposed to do, or rather, what my duties were in keeping with the rules and regulations. And then the next one was whether I wrote an order. And then there were some other questions included. I don't think I can answer your questions in this way. Please, if we can go question by question, I'll try to answer every single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an intelligence support order, what that is or what that might be? Are you familiar with it, the concept?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I'm familiar with what an intelligence support order is and everything surrounding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in fact, in your own -- in the intelligence support manual, Article 259 gives a description of what -- of the plan and of the order. The order is in 263. So if you could look at 259, and then Article 263, in the intelligence support manual which has been premarked for identification purposes as D14/1.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dated 1987. Is that the one you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please just tell me which item.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's 259. This whole chapter deals with intelligence documents. 259 talks about plan --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Karnavas, may I just have a minute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 259.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe the third paragraph, it talks about what needs to be in the intelligence support plan.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Karnavas, go ahead and ask your question. I've looked through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please also look at 263 further down, or just give it a quick look. I'm sure you should be familiar with these rules.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, if you could be so kind as to flip over to look at the forms. I believe in the English version, it would be page 93 and 94. That would be the form for the plan. And then on 96, it's the form of an order. And again, that's D14/1 for identification purposes. Have you looked at those forms? You're shaking your head. Does that mean yes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know which these forms are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, having refreshed your memory, or at least knowing exactly what I'm talking about, let's discuss what an intelligence support order is. Is it not a document that you are supposed to prepare? That's one of your functions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've understood your question. If I was supposed to prepare an order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. As part of your -- when you are the intelligence -- the head of the intelligence organ, okay, forget about security, intelligence, is not one of your functions to prepare an order, an intelligence support order, along with that order attach a detailed plan as shown in the form? Is that not one of your functions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this was not quite the way you said it. The way in which you have described I was supposed to do it is not true. I can explain exactly what the procedure is, what the stages of the process are, what is done and who signs this. So it was not the way you described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First, my question is: Is it not your responsibility to draft it? Yes or no? The order and the plan. And then we'll talk about the procedure. I just want to know who drafts it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, my responsibility was to take part in all the different stages before the commander adopts a decision. My responsibility was to take part in the drafting of documents by the intelligence organ which also includes the documents that you have been referring to. What you are speaking about are intelligence-organ documents, documents written and filed by the intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is the answer to my question yes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after you've drafted it, your commander is supposed to look at it and decide whether he's going to approve it or not, give his approval?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document are you referring to precisely?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What are we talking about, Mr. Nikolic, the intelligence support order, the intelligence support plan that you've just drafted. That's what I'm talking about. After you prepare it, do you not share it as you must under the rules with your commander so he can look at it and see whether he's is going to approve it? Isn't that a fact? Isn't that part of the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, we spoke about two different documents. We spoke about the plan on the one hand and the intelligence support order on the other. I was just asking you which of these two documents you were asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, let me break it down. Let's start from the beginning. After an order such as the one prepared by your commander on the 5th of July, 1995, after such an order is prepared, is it not one of your functions, is not one of your functions to prepare a more comprehensive intelligence support order based on the commander's order?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, part of that order, attached to it, is a detailed plan as specified in the form, fill in the blanks, easy, as is the form. That goes along with the order. So you got the plan, and you got the order. Or you can say you got the order, and then you look at the plan. So you have initially the order prepared by the commander, you then prepare an order, attach a plan to it, then send it back - share it - to your commander so he can look at it and decide whether he's going to approve of it or not, make some changes or adopt it as is, or maybe send it back and say "redraft it." Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer by using just one word, whether this is correct or not. I write the order for intelligence security, and I forward all orders to the commander, including that one. Speaking of the intelligence support plan, I would be the one to draft it as the chief of intelligence and security affairs organ. I would submit this to the commander, and then the commander would approve this order and sign it. Depending on the form of the document, he would approve the document or sign the document at any rate, the commander had the final word on the intelligence support order. Then it's drafted for the unit I belonged to, for the brigade. And of course, the intelligence support order is also drafted for -- and copied for the subordinate units. And it is true that I do all these things. Pursuant to that order, a document is drawn up, a plan, for intelligence support where the forces needed and the equipment needed are defined, and anything else that's included in the form. This document, too, is approved and signed by the commander. However, Mr. Karnavas, I must add the following: In order for me to do all of this, in order for me to draft the plan and the order, I must be familiar, first of all, with the commander's decision. I must know what his decision is. I must know what the commander has decided in order for me to be able to write the order and the intelligence support plan. Unless I have the commander's decision, Mr. Karnavas, all of this can also be done and based on the commander's general idea or plan. But first, I must be familiar with this general idea or plan. If the commander doesn't tell me what the general idea is, if he doesn't familiarise me with this, if he doesn't show me the order in which he defines this general idea, then it is impossible for me to write any document because I am simply not aware of the commander's decision. So this is the essential explanation concerning these documents. It is true, Mr. Karnavas, that I write, prepare, and submit to the commander these documents for approval. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And once again, Mr. Nikolic, I think you made it painfully clear that you were not involved in the initial drafting of the order of 5 July 1995. I got that point. But as I understand it, after the commander approves and signs the intelligence support order with the attached plan, then and only then are you allowed to send it directly to your other -- to your higher-ups in the intelligence community, that is, at the core? You're sending the report, are you not, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, these documents were not documents that were based on -- that the reports were based on. These were combat documents of the brigade itself. These were combat documents of the commander. These were combat-related documents of a brigade engaged in combat operations. I must apologise again. I must remind you, you made a mistake there. A request is written and sent to the superior command. You have it right there in the rules, a request for intelligence. A request is written if you need to find out about something that is not for you to know or within your purview, within your area of work. You would then send a request to the neighbouring unit, and that would have been the only document sent straight to the corps command. So these documents are combat-related documents of the brigade. They remain in a file there. They form part of a file. And then all those documents together form a group of documents based on which the commander makes his decisions. It is not sent anywhere. Combat orders for intelligence support are sent to subordinate units. In our case, this would be sent to battalions, the 1st, the 2nd, 3rd, and the 4th battalion would receive orders related to the intelligence security by their superior command, and their superior command would have been the 1st Bratunac Brigade Light Infantry Brigade. And then orders are received to reconnoiter. These would also be drawn up by myself, approved or signed by the commander, and then these orders would be sent on to the reconnaissance platoon of the brigade. But all these documents remain within the brigade, and these documents are not reported because the corps command, as applies to its own level of work, also has and writes such documents. So this kind of document isn't sent anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So let me give you a hypothetical. Had the -- your commander, had your commander shared with you his order which you have stated repeatedly you've never seen and was not aware of, but had he shared this with you, your next task prior to the attack on Srebrenica would have been to prepare an intelligence support order with a detailed plan. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Karnavas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there, what you would be doing is sort of putting meat to the skeleton of the original order drafted by your commander, because after all you're the expert service, you're the expert in this intelligence field. So you would be writing the details in that plan with the order which would dovetail what the commander had in his initial plan.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Are you entitled to put in your plan whatever you feel like it, or must you follow the general outline that was prepared by your commander in his order? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, my commander does not set out the details within the frameworks of those measures. So in principle, he asks his associates, including myself, in principle, he sets the task. But I'm the commanding officer who did that kind of work, so I don't need the commander, that's the kind of work I was trained for. I don't need the commander to write out five pages for me. All he needs to do is write a single sentence, and then it is clear to me what my job is. So then I go about my own business, my own work. I say myself, but all the other assistants to the commander go about their own business because they are all people who are trained for this kind of work, they have undergone training, professional and so on, and they know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was trying to convey. I apologise for being inarticulate. Now, am I to understand or are we to understand that with respect to the July 5, 1995, order, had it been shared with you and had you gone ahead and drafted an intelligence support order with a plan and had your commander approved and signed it, it would not be distributed to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, they are combat documents belonging to the brigade, and they're not send often further to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So that the intelligence, the intelligence officers at the corps would not have access to this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence officers of the corps, of the superior command, can always come if the need arises, and then they receive an order or anything else. So they can have access to the documents and see them. It's no secret, especially for the corps commanding officers who compile their own documents at their own level, the same ones at their own level. So on the basis of those documents and the definition of the requirements, so that is the guiding light for the organs in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if the corps wanted to figure out, the corps security -- intelligence, the corps intelligence wanted to know what the Bratunac Brigade intelligence was doing, they would have to humble themselves to Bratunac, come to you or to the headquarters, and look at what documents, what intelligence support order and plan was drafted and approved by the commander. So the higher command comes down to the lower command to find out what it's doing based on the orders it has issued. Is that how it works? I just want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. That is not how it works at all, especially when we're talking about these documents and what we were just discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But as far as you're concerned, the corps intelligence office, the higher command, would only have access to those documents if they had asked for them to be sent up to them or if they had come to the brigade. But you, as the intelligence officer, after the plan and the order was approved by the commander had absolutely no obligation to send it up. That's your position? Just so we're clear. Think about it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have thought about it, Mr. Karnavas. As far as this question goes and these observations of yours, they don't hold water. They're absolutely not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the brigade writes his order in the spirit of the order issued by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whereas I, I myself as the chief of the intelligence security organ also write out all these documents in the spirit of the order given and in conformity with the point in the order of the Drina Corps commander and on the basis of the decision taken by my own commander, which means there's no need for us to go about this process as you have described it and control of information because it follows down a line, from the corps commander down to the brigade commander, the order of the brigade commander is in the spirit of the order given by the corps commander. My information security is concretised in my area of responsibility, the area of responsibility of my own brigade. So this is the kind of work and process that combines all this and gets its spirit from the planning level to the elaboration of the actual documents. So I did not say you wanted to put that in my lips, that they have to humble themselves, the ones at the top, to humble themselves to go down to the lower level to take a look at the documents, that is to say, the corps commander down to my organ. They are commanding officers who are superior to me in the professional sense. And with respect to all questions defined by the rules of service for the security organs, and I am duty-bound to report back to the commanding officers of the corps, whereas they, for their part, have the right to come to the brigade command and headquarters whenever they feel like it to control all the documents and have an insight into the documents that I am compiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if I understand the process as you have described it, once the commander of the Bratunac Brigade prepares his report in the spirit of the Drina Corps order, he doesn't have to share it. He doesn't have to send it up to the Drina Corps for them to look at to make sure that it is indeed in the spirit of the order that was initially issued. If I understand the process as you've described it, that's what you seem to be saying.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, no, I didn't -- you're going further and further and putting words into my mouth, things I didn't say at all. Now you're talking about the order by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nikolic, if I may interrupt you. You were talking about the stages, you said it goes from up, further down, further down. And I didn't hear you say that the orders have to go back up. Maybe I missed that point. That's why I asked you. After your intelligence support order and plan is approved by the commander, aren't you required - required - not an option, required - to send it to the higher command so that they know exactly what the intelligence organ in the lower command, their subordinates, are doing? Because after all, this is a battle. They need to be coordinated. They need to know where everybody else is. They need to have information coming. So isn't it a fact, isn't it a fact that you would have to send it? It's not a trick question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. I take it that you did not prepare an intelligence support order and plan based on the 5 July 1995 order that was drafted by your commander.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the reason for that was because you were unaware of his order?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we have a forward command post in Pribicevac, which is -- by car, how long would it take to go there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. It's about 25 kilometres away from Bratunac. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it since it was a forward command post, it would have a communication facility or means, communication means; that is, so that the people that are back at the headquarters can contact the folks at the forward command post, especially if the commander is there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it's my understanding that when you are in an active-battle situation and where you have a forward command post, either the commander or it could be the chief of staff, one of them, will go to the forward command post, and the other will remain in the command post, in the headquarters, so that in case something does happen, you don't have both the commander and the chief of staff gone all at once. I mean, that's the basic principle. I mean, I'm oversimplifying things, but isn't that how it's normally done?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not any kind of rule. I don't know whether that's how it's done or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll get to that later. Now, we know that -- I know, but I don't know. Do you know whether Colonel Blagojevic was in Pribicevac during those days, at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that Colonel Blagojevic was -- if you're asking me at the beginning or rather you're asking me during the attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During the attack, between the 6th and the 11th, did you know where he was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know. I knew that Colonel Blagojevic was at Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we established that you had a car, so I take it you were -- you could have gone to visit him if you wanted to. I don't know if you did, but you could have. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have, Mr. Karnavas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You could have picked up the phone or the communication means that were available to communicate with him and say "hey, commander, what's going on? I understand we have a battle going on." You could have done that. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure whether I could have had that kind of communication. But let's say for argument purposes that I could have, because you're asking a hypothetical, so my answer is a hypothetical, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You mean -- okay, well, I want to stick with this a little bit if you don't mind. Are you trying to tell me that if you needed to communicate with your commander from wherever you were, you could not do so, while he was in Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I'm concerned, me personally, if that's what you're asking me, I could have communicated with the commander from the communications centre, the communications centre of the Bratunac Brigade, in fact. But I didn't have any means by which to communicate at this distance of 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand that one. But all right, let me move on. Now, since the commander was there in Pribicevac, it would stand to reason that the chief of staff who, under the rules, directly controls you - now, we can quiver about that, but that's what the rules say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The chief of staff was in the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at that time whether he was or wasn't. Possibly he was, but I really can't say. I don't know. I don't exclude the possibility of him being there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Help me out here. His office is on the second floor like your office. Is that correct? They call it first floor here in Europe. Ground floor, next floor.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was. Actually, my office was at one entrance to the building, and his office was on quite -- in quite the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All the way at the other end?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as we said yesterday, the folks that owned the factory had put up the walls, and you couldn't go down the corridor, you couldn't look through and you couldn't walk through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. We did say that yesterday for a long time, and I don't -- asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this point becomes significant because this gentleman claims that he has seen lots of things. We had Ruez on the stand who after five or six years of investigation never went into the building, didn't know how the building looked, couldn't tell us which offices were where, and I think it's a relevant point. And the point I am trying to make is where the office was for the chief of staff and whether this gentleman knew it at the time so he could be able to find it and maybe even speak with the chief of staff had he so chosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that is a relevant point. You may proceed along this line, but, Mr. Karnavas, if you finish this part of the cross-examination, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Couple minutes, Your Honour. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you could not walk down that corridor because there was a wall on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying it. Are you trying to tell me that you could walk straight through down to your commander's office without having to go downstairs, around, and up a flight of stairs? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please describe for us the Bratunac Brigade headquarters as you knew it at that particular time. Tell us exactly what was on the ground floor, what was on the top floor, and who was where, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I am going to tell you what I remember best. The command of the Bratunac Brigade was in the building of a socially owned enterprise called Kaolin from Bratunac. It's a building which is situated approximately 500 to 600 metres from the town centre moving in the direction from Bratunac to Kravica and Konjevic Polje. It's on that road, and 500 metres from there. From Bratunac, 500 metres later, you turn left and you come to the command of the Bratunac Brigade. The building itself is rectangular shape. It's a long building. And there's an asphalt road in front of it. It's a concrete building I think made of concrete blocks. And when you enter from the direction you're coming from, that is, the street entrance, you go straight in at an angle of 90 degrees, or roughly so, perhaps a little to the left. There's the kitchen on the ground floor, the kitchens. Then to the left, we have the warehouse or storage space. In the left-hand entrance, on the ground-floor level, I think that was the office of the commander of the post of the Bratunac Brigade and perhaps some auxiliary staff. I don't know exactly. And in that left-hand corner when you go up the stairs and to the right, to the end of the corridor was my office. And for a time, there was an empty office. It was vacant. Nobody used it. I don't know what purpose it served later on. So when you go up the stairs in that part of the building and turn left, or rather, you go -- there's an office straight ahead. But that's where the offices were, the assistant chief of staff or commander for organisational matters and personnel matters. That was -- they used one, two, or three offices, the assistant and his clerks. Then further down that same corridor, you would find the offices for the assistant commander for logistics and his staff and clerks. Further down the corridor still, when you enter the entrance where my office is, along that corridor was the communications centre. I think they used a large hall in actual fact, and another room where the encryption took place and the documents were sent out. So unless I've forgotten something, those were the premises. And on the left-hand side -- on the left-hand side of the building and the entrance where my office was located. Now, on the right-hand side of the building, so when you look at the building, coming to the building, on the right-hand side, the last entrance there, you would go into that entrance. And then several steps into the building and into the corridor, you would enter an area, a space where the operative hall was, operations room was. And then there's an office there now with clerks from the operational and educational sector or something like that. Whether they were there all the time, I don't know. Now, entering the corridor, you go up the stairs and come to the floor. Let's call it the second floor or first floor, whichever you like. This upper-storey level, to the left as you come up the stairs, you would find the brigade commander's office. Or rather, the chief of staff's office was also a dormitory next to the commander. I remember that he used this for a time with Lieutenant Micic in the operational and educational hall. That's where they worked, spent some time and so on. Later on, there might have been some changes to all this. But I have described it to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you walk from your office on that floor directly to see your commander? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- rather, walking through the corridor, I couldn't go directly to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because there was a wall on your side, and there was a wall on the other side further down separating your section from where the commander and the chief of staff's section was because that's how this state-owned enterprise wanted it to be. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a wall because in the state-owned enterprise, or rather, while the command of the Bratunac Brigade was located in that building, that state-owned enterprise -- the owners of the factory, in fact, used part of the premises to store their documents and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. They didn't want the military using -- taking over the entire building, so this was one way of trying to keep part of the building for themselves. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So as I asked earlier, in order to get from your office to where the chief of staff or your commander was, you'd have to walk down a flight of stairs, go around the building, go through the entrance that's on the far right side, up a stair flight, and right around in that area is where your commander and your chief of staff had their offices. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour, for right now, before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have the break. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, where were you on the 6th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of July, 1995, I was in the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably in the area of command of the Bratunac Brigade, the headquarters, somewhere in town, in that general area. I don't think I could be more accurate. I can't specify in which place I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could the answer also be "most probably not at the forward command post in Pribicevac"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of July, you could say that I wasn't in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because, in fact, you were not in that area, at the Pribicevac forward command post of the Bratunac Brigade where your commander was on the day of the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that, Mr. Karnavas. One could say that on the 6th, I was not there. But in the previous days throughout that period and earlier, I had been to the forward command post at Pribicevac, and I know exactly where this place is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the previous days. But we'll get to that as well. I'm talking about the 6th. Now, let's go on to the 7th. On the 7th, where were you, Mr. Nikolic? What did you do on that day, the 7th of July, 1995, the second day of the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th, Mr. Karnavas, to the best of my recollection, I don't think I ever left Bratunac. I don't think I was permanently engaged anywhere, not in any of the battalions, not in any of the subordinate units, the units subordinate to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what about the 8th? July 8th, 1995. To the best of your recollection, where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, one could state with certainty that I was at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, probably going to the military police building in town, spending time in my office. All in all, those were the usual places where I was throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The military police building in town, is that a separate building from the one that is about 20 or 30 metres in front of the Bratunac Brigade headquarters? Or is that the same one that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police building was not in the same building as the brigade headquarters. It was a separate prefab building where the military police were stationed, where their offices were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's about a 60-second walk from the one building to the next building?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you said with certainty, one could say -- could state with certainty that you were in town, in Bratunac. Could we also say with certainty that you were not in Pribicevac on that particular day, the 8th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I didn't go to Pribicevac in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So that would have included the previous day, the 7th. I failed to ask you that question. I just want to lock you in -- make sure I understand where you were. So the 7th you weren't there. The 8th you weren't there. The 9th you were not at Pribicevac. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the 10th, you were not in Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about on the 11th? You weren't there either, were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during that period, your commander, the one that you were to report to at least directly with respect to security matters, was at Pribicevac in his forward command post during the attack on Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had information that throughout that period, he was staying at the forward command post in Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during this period, from the 6th, the 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, you had no contact with your commander. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I had no physical contact with my commander, and it is true that I didn't communicate with him over the phone. As far as I remember, there were no calls or requests made by the commander, nor did I have any problems in that period or received any requests from the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So let me ask you this question: In the history of the Bratunac Brigade, from the time that it was formed back in 1992 until Srebrenica, would it be fair to say that the attack on Srebrenica was the most significant event for the Bratunac Brigade, if not for the Drina Corps as well, and maybe even the main staff? I don't know. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, all I can give you is my opinion. I think one could confirm what you just said; it was a crucial attack, very important both for the brigade and for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, the Drina Corps in drafting a very specific order based on orders from the higher-up had mobilised various units in order to organise this military campaign, this battle, the purpose of which was to shrink the areas of Srebrenica -- the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you have asked several questions again in one. It is true -- I can indeed confirm that the Drina Corps had mobilised, if you mean mobilise as in assembled in one place, because the mobilisation process had been over by that time. Long over, in fact. They assembled some of the units, some of their own units to carry out this task. This is indeed true, and I can confirm this. I know this. Can you please repeat the second part of your question. I'm not sure what it referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I stand corrected in the use of "mobilisation," assemble. You're absolutely correct. They had assembled all these different units. And the battle plan, as I understand it from reading the order, had a particular purpose which was to shrink the enclave of Srebrenica, not to take it over. And I think we established that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, when we discussed this particular issue, I must say that I've spoken about this already, and I told you that I knew the goal of the attack on Srebrenica. And before I received documents from the Prosecution and familiarised myself with certain orders, I knew that the goal of the attack on Srebrenica was to separate the enclaves. However, I didn't know what the objective of the further attack would be, to shrink, as you say, the enclave and all the other aims as they were defined. That's as much as I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But needless to say, needless to say, on this historic, momentous occasion, however you wish to put it, on the history of the Bratunac Brigade, you Momir Nikolic, the head of the intelligence and security sector, as you stand here today, assert that you were totally excluded by your own commander.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas, I did not say this. All I can confirm here is that I was not excluded from it. I can also say that my commander, very close to the actual date when the attack on Srebrenica was carried out, gave an evaluation of my work. My commander was fully familiar with my activities. Your Honours, Mr. Karnavas wants to know about this, and he assumes that my commander had excluded me from everything. We should look at a document showing the analysis of combat readiness stating exactly what I did and what my tasks were, how the tasks and my carrying out of those tasks were evaluated. This is a document by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Mr. Karnavas. May we now look at this document, Your Honours, to verify that I was absolutely not excluded from anything and that I did everything that I had been tasked to do throughout the period preceding the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the word "excluded" may be the right word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday you indicated that under the rules and the ongoing practice and procedure, when it comes to drafting an order such as this one of the July 5th, 1995 plan that was drafted by your commander, it is customary, and the rules make that clear, that you should be consulted and make a proposal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He doesn't have to accept the proposal, but at least he has to -- not has to, but he should allow you, because after all, you are the expert in the area, to give him your expert advice so he can put it into the plan. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And based on that, we talked today that you would then prepare an additional order, an intelligence support order, with a plan based on the order drafted by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In this particular instance, in this particular instance with respect to the battle plan on Srebrenica, you, Momir Nikolic, the chief of intelligence and security, were not consulted?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, you were not even shared -- a copy was not even -- a courtesy copy was not even distributed to you, the chief of intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course, since you didn't know that this existed - or you might have - but obviously you never saw it, you never followed up on what might have been expected of you, and that is, in drafting an intelligence support order with an attached plan to it. Once again, being cut out of the process, being excluded. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this is true as concerns the drafting of those documents. But may I just be allowed to clarify the following: What you are talking about, meaning the consequence of all the things that you have been talking about, that I was no part of this, that I did not receive an order, that I was not familiar with it, this means that I could not draft written documents attached to the commander's report concerning the carrying out of combat operations. This means I could not have written that, which doesn't mean, Mr. Karnavas, that if I was unable to write up two or three documents or orders approved by the commander, this doesn't mean that I ceased to carry out my intelligence and security duties. It doesn't mean that I ceased to communicate with my subordinates. I continued my work. But as for this specific operation, I was not in a position to write up the plan to be attached to the detailed analysis and report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely. You were not part of the process. Just with this order, that's all I'm talking about. I'm not talking about whether you carried out your functions with your subordinates. We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I was not part of the process that related to the compiling of combat documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And also, even though you knew, even though you knew that the Bratunac Brigade was engaged in this operation, albeit to the extent designated on this particular order, you made no effort to ask your commander or the chief of staff for a copy of the order which had to have existed. You must have known that something must have existed because you just don't show up one day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just this had several questions in it, and I believe we went over this in detail already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to get a final answer on this question alone, Your Honour, and then I'll move on. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, there were about four, five questions in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'll break it down, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, try to ask a simple question because -- I think that's because of the problem of translation, you know. Some ideas are very clear in English, but when it's translated into B/C/S, there might arise, you know, different understandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I truly apologise, Your Honour. I'll keep working on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could briefly state, the other concern I have is that when there is a two- or three-part question and there's an assumed fact in it, like he did a while back saying "you reported as the security person" and then he asked a question, I can see that we all like to use our in our trial briefs. And when something like that gets used in argument, it makes it look like the witness has answered a particular part of the question, when if there's two or three parts, it's really hard to figure out what he's answering. So, I don't want to interrupt the every time, but it's going to be very hard to make anything from the record when there's several questions in each question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's my understanding from listening to you that throughout this period, the 6th, the 7th, the 8th, the 9th, the 10th, the 11th, even though you did not see the order, and you did not communicate with your commander, you were nonetheless carrying out all of your functions, both under the intelligence and the security sector. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say yes because again, you are stating something that is not quite true. I was carrying out my duties under the intelligence and the security sector. I was carrying out those tasks which according to my estimate at that time were priority tasks that needed carrying out. I wasn't carrying out all the tasks. I was just carrying out the tasks that were deemed priority in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Self-managing. Might that be a good way of characterising what you were doing? You were self-managing your time; you were setting the priorities.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Karnavas, I must say that you have either misunderstood me or I'm not getting the correct interpretation. I was not setting my own priorities. The priorities were defined by the situation. In a specific situation, the situation unfolding, my own activities would be defined.
