So in my understanding, this is the role for units, battalions, companies, and so on and so forth. In this sense, what I said is that the task in my understanding, and based on what conclusions I can draw from the rules of service, this would have been no police task, the one on which the military police platoon is apparently being deployed here. I said something else, too. I believe -- if I had suggested to use military police, I would never have suggested to the commander that this military police platoon under the circumstances should be used as a reserve unit. I think I said something roughly to that effect. And I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could look at Articles 22, 23, 24, and 25, if you could just look at them very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 22 you said, the first one? 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 22, 23, 24, and 25, if you could just look at them.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I understand it correctly, the commander, the brigade commander, your commander, was entitled to use the military police in his brigade as he saw fit as long as the usage was within the confines of the rules. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commander always has the right to decide to use the military police platoon, be it within the rules or outside the rules. He always has this right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be not be correct to state that in reading Article 22 in conjunction, say, with Article 23 or perhaps Article 24, which deals with situations where war is envisaged, that the use of a military police platoon as a reserve can be appropriate under the rules, if deemed necessary by the commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, we're talking about Article 22, tasks of the military police, they refer to peacetime tasks. I haven't finished reading this. There's plenty to read through. But from what I've seen, military police in peacetime shall carry out the following tasks. So these should then be peacetime tasks. I can't comment on that because we're not talking about peacetime right now. Article 23, in addition to tasks enumerated in Article 22, peacetime tasks, in extraordinary circumstances, the military police execute the following tasks --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in addition to 22 --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't quite finished, Mr. Karnavas. May I just be allowed to complete my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, go for it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, in addition to tasks enumerated in Item 22, Item 23 of this rule define tasks in extraordinary circumstances, what the military police are to do. I hope we are talking about extraordinary circumstances. In my opinion, it was war. It was wartime. There was a state of war in point of fact. Item 25, or rather 24, I think you told me, the next one, may I just have a minute to find it. 23. Item 24: In addition to the tasks from Items 22 and 23, that means peacetime and extraordinary circumstances, the military police also execute the following tasks during an imminent threat of war and mobilisation. Again, this is an article or item not defining tasks for the military police in wartime. These are not wartime tasks. This only talks about mobilisation. This is still not war. This is short of war. Units are being mobilised, and the military police have special tasks to carry out regarding the mobilisation of units. Article or Item 25, in addition to the tasks from items 22 to 24 of this rule, in wartime the military police also execute the following tasks. Of course, it's all that I've already mentioned, directly provide for the security of the command post, commander of the military unit or institution, take part in preventing the activities by any armed enemy groups or individuals that have been infiltrated, take part in controlling and ensuring on security measures, regulated in order in the areas awaiting collection and embarkation, disembarkation, implement the orders for banning or limiting movement in certain directions and areas, provide security for allied military missions and delegations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you are too fast. You are too fast. It's impossible for the typist to follow you. I don't think there's any need to read the whole article. We all know that in Article 25, it is stated very clearly in wartime. You may stop here, and Mr. Karnavas will give you some directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you go down to f, it talks about the military police taking part in directing the movement of refugees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, take part in directing the movements of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And then on h, and we talked about this yesterday a little bit, about providing security for prisoners of war in camps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we go to Article 57, it states: "The military police may also, upon a special order, escort prisoners of war." Do you see where it says "special order"? One line, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've found it. I can see that. Item 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in looking at -- in looking at the -- going back to the order itself of July 5, 1995, if you go to paragraph 10 - for the record, I'm referring to the D17/1 - it designates as the area of collecting of prisoners of war and loot in the area of Pribicevac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just please repeat the number. Right, I've found it. Maybe not. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you have to tell the witness in which paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought he said he found it. It's paragraph 10 under A where it says "intelligence and security," and there's one, two, three, four, five. And it says, we talked about this yesterday, "the area of collecting of POWs and loot in the area of Pribicevac. Apply Geneva Convention in treatment of POWs and population." Do you see that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still looking for it. The area of collecting of POW, yes, the Pribicevac area, yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's where your commander had designated the area where POWs would be collected, according to this order. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when the order was drafted, which was 5 July 1995, would it be fair to assume that no one expected Srebrenica to fall?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't draw any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether someone expected something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Being the intelligence officer that you were, the chief of security and intelligence, with all of your resources and subordinates feeding you that information that you were funneling around and deciding whether you would give it to your commander or not, did you know at the time what role exactly the Bratunac Brigade was going to play in the attack on Srebrenica? Yes, no, maybe? Pick one of the three.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew, Mr. Karnavas, that the Bratunac Brigade would be one of the participants in the attack on Srebrenica. I've said this countless times, and I will say it again. I have not seen this order. I have never read it. I could not have known what the commander had assigned as tasks to battalion commanders, not precisely what. I knew they would take part in the attack. I knew the composition of the brigade, what those units were. But how, carrying what tasks exactly, I couldn't have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can I take it as a security -- the chief, the chief of the security during that five- or six-day period you never figured it out whether they were playing a major offensive role or whether they were maintaining their line more or less and perhaps providing some assistance? You never figured that one out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a demeaning, badgering style of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the manner of the question may be not good, but there's a point in this question. Maybe, Mr. Karnavas, you could rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will do that. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You had -- is it your position today, being the chief of intelligence and security of the Bratunac Brigade that from the 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, and 11th, throughout that whole period, you never figured out exactly what role the Bratunac Brigade was going to play in the attack on Srebrenica? Is that what you're telling us here today, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not claiming this the way you have just defined it. I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know -- do you know whether -- did you know, did you know back then, the 5th, the 6th, the 7th, the 8th, the 9th, the 10th, the 11th, that Pribicevac was going to be the place that the POWs were supposed to be gathered, the ones that were captured by the Bratunac Brigade? Did you know that? Pretty simple.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. I didn't know it was Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Might I conclude, might I conclude that you never made any efforts to find out where the POWs would be gathered if indeed the Bratunac Brigade were to capture any POWs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I didn't ask questions about where the POWs would be. According to my information, which was only to be expected, and according to my estimate, if I had been consulted, the normal thing would have been to gather POWs in the zones of responsibility of the respective battalions. That would have been normal, usual, in view of the deployment of the brigade's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. But in Pribicevac, the forward command post of the Bratunac Brigade was the location where the commander of the brigade had chosen where he would be during this campaign process. Does it not make sense to you that perhaps the commander would want to be near, in the vicinity where any prisoners might be captured to ensure, one, their security, and two, whether they may have any intelligence information that might assist the Bratunac Brigade or the Drina Corps in this campaign, in the attack of Srebrenica? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I don't have the slightest intention of commenting on this decision. The decision was made by the brigade commander. The assessment was his. I believe it is completely pointless to ask me for my opinion on this. This was a decision taken by the commander. As I said in my testimony yesterday, regardless of what I believed, regardless of what I proposed, if the commander made a decision clearly defined in a written order, then there was nothing else for me to say or to think. It was not for me to think then. If the commander binds me to act in keeping with the order, there were no further comments for me to make. That was the commander's decision. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could, and I hate to do this, but if we could just go back just one last time to the intelligence support, and I want you to look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's, for the record, D14/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could look at Article 198, perhaps that may give us some guidance as to what your role might have been with respect to prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, point 191 -- 198 did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 198. And let me read it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find it, if I may take a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does it not say: "Intelligence organs in commands" --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I haven't found it yet. Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. "Intelligence organs in commands and staff question prisoners of war and defectors for the purpose of gathering intelligence, through organs of certain specialty that are set up especially for that purpose." Now, help me out here, Mr. Nikolic. You were the head of the intelligence organ, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. We're dealing with intelligence right now. Thank you for reminding me. Now, according to 198, it would seem to be that your function during those days would have been, at least one of your functions would have been to be available to question prisoners of war in order to collect intelligence information. Is that correct? That would have been your function?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, one of the sources of intelligence is to question prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then on 199 it says -- it talks about the principles which you have to adhere to in questioning them. In 200, we see again the application of the Geneva Conventions, annex 1. In other words, you have to comply with that. And in fact, lest there be any mistakes, it's annexed. You have it in the rules itself, the relevant sections of the Geneva Conventions. So as I understand your testimony today, you did not see this order that was drafted by your commander, nor were you aware of what was in the order itself during the 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, and 11th of July 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that I wasn't informed with that order and that I did not know what was defined, or rather in this command. I did not know what was defined in the commander order in the area that I was responsible for, intelligence and intelligence security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One of your responsibilities would have been, would have been, to question any prisoners of war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I've already answered that question. But what I should like to say is this: Something else in connection with this question, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before you launch into your dialogue, could you please answer my question. Would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answered your question. Yes, one of my tasks would be to question prisoners of war, the prisoners of war who are brought to the Bratunac Brigade or I would appear on the spot. But yes, what you say is absolutely correct, that one of my task would be to question the prisoners of war. Now, what I want to say is this, because you asked me something else with respect to a concrete order and a concrete position: I, or rather the brigade in all the battalions, including the 3rd infantry battalion, whose area of responsibility was Pribicevac, and the command post at Pribicevac. I had an assistant, the commander for intelligence and security affairs, an assistant, a commander of the battalion for intelligence and security affairs, for which -- for whom I claim now, and I have a document here, a report, that that particular assistant was trained and professionally equipped to perform those duties in the battalion. And he is the person who, in the area of his responsibility, that is to say, the 3rd infantry battalion, will gather because he knows what his duties and tasks are. Gather up the prisoners, secure them up there, to question them as far as he is able to do so. And once they arrive to the brigade headquarters or to any spot designated for them to be gathered together and secured, then if the need arises, I can go there perhaps, or my clerk, somebody from the organ, to question them. And that would be the normal standard procedure. So, Mr. Karnavas, it is not my duty, wherever a prisoner crops up in a battalion, to rush off to Pribicevac to question that particular prisoner, and then to go back, to hurry back. I have my organs, my assistants in this chain of command who are already there and who can do that. And the commander can avail himself of those services at any time during the day and night. If the need arises, if there is new intelligence which he finds necessary in order to make his decisions with respect to the deployment of forces along that particular axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you through?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have completed what I wanted to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did your assistant by any chance inform you that there was a battle going on to take Srebrenica and to inform you what the orders were, just out of curiosity? Was he able to pass that information on to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that the question is -- or rather, that it's a question that I would have to answer because there's no sense nor need for the assistant commander for intelligence and security from the battalion to inform me that operations are underway. That is something I knew about it, and I said that, Mr. Karnavas. So I know there was fighting going on. I know there were battles going on. And I said that I knew roughly the role played by the battalion. What I said was that I didn't know the exact deployment and specific tasks and assignments, the facilities and so I don't know the details. However, you are now trying to say that the assistant commander for intelligence and security should have informed me. I know about all that. I knew about all that, all the things that you're bringing up now. I was aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Did you ask him by any chance to help you find the order so you could look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, we come back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one last point regarding this order, dealing with 5.5, if you could look at 5.5 on the order of July 5, 1995. I want to -- I'd like you to focus on the first line. Earlier when I questioned you --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to point 5. What was the other number?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, as I understood your testimony earlier, you did not know what those letters meant, the L/r, and the tt. And you asked me to provide you with that information. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked you what this abbreviation meant, although I have my own opinions as to what it means. But yes, of course, I did ask you because I wasn't quite clear on what the abbreviation stood for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how about "line of development" for the L/r? Linija razvoya. I believe that's -- I'm giving, taking a shot at it in your language. R-a-z-v-o-y-a. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Line of development, linija razvoya, doesn't mean, or line of deployment of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or line of deployment. Is not that what this means?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that could mean anything in actual fact, although it could also mean the reconnaissance platoon of a brigade, one which had rocket launchers, Mr. Karnavas. It could mean anything and everything. I really don't know what this applies to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about the "tt"? Does that not mean elevation point or --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, trigonometry point or elevation point, yes, elevation quota.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now that I refreshed your memory or rejuvenated it, isn't it a fact, Mr. Nikolic, that a squad leader, a squad leader, would be able to look at this, this order, read this line, and be able to interpret that? Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, the squad leader never receives an order. I don't know whether he would be able to read this. But he doesn't get the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we do know one thing: The chief of intelligence and security under oath here either claims not to be able to read an order or just doesn't know how to read an order. That we do know for a fact, don't we, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. I didn't say I wasn't able to read the order, nor did I say what you just now said. What I said was that I didn't have an opportunity of seeing this particular order, and I did not know what the tasks were which were defined within the frameworks of this order and which related to me. That is what I said on countless occasions so far here. And I repeat it again, and that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour. I think I made the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wanted to clear up one thing on this order. There has been an implication on the Blagojevic order. That order has never been seen by the Prosecution. I do not believe it was part of the Prosecution collection. And if -- I know counsel is helping us try to find where they got it. And at this point, I just wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. McCloskey, I believe that you have a chance to pursue this issue during your rebuttal period. And Mr. Karnavas, before we leave this subject, could you tell us the source of this document, I mean just to lay some foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour as far as we know, and I've communicated this to Mr. McCloskey himself, that he received him from him. And we have been looking to try to find exactly in which of the disks. We've received close to 5 million pages of documents. We have a Zylab system, we are looking, Mr. McCloskey knows this, and he knows we are acting in good faith, and I'm rather outraged that he would stand up here and say he does not know where this came from or it didn't come from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, it's useless to blame each other. The issue is that we have to know the source. We have to know some basic foundations of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could not agree with you more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I hope after Court, you could do more research on this issue before we finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And inform us about the source of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. And to repeat again, we have been spent about three days -- I will spend the weekend looking for this. We will try to find this within the disclosure material because we did not get it from any other source, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I hope so. If I am going to tender it, I will need to lay a foundation. I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am perfectly familiar with the Rules of Evidence as they exist in the Tribunal. And I will lay a foundation if I cannot find the source, but I am confident that we will be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I only hope my ruling won't ruin your weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your ruling will probably be after my weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, yesterday, you indicated that as far as you understood, this order was still in existence on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course the order was in existence. I assume throughout the whole time because it was an order for combat action. I think that was the title and heading. There weren't any others during that period of time. Although perhaps there were. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether the Bratunac Brigade received any other orders, written orders, from the Drina Corps subsequent to the fall of Srebrenica? Let me rephrase. I withdraw the question. Why don't I show you a document which we received from the Prosecution. It's dated July 13th. And it comes from the Drina Corps. And if I can locate the identification number here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is that D28?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. That is correct. I must be getting tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could look at this order and see if you can recognise it or read it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- do you know what -- could you please identify what the document is.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the header, we can see that the document is being sent from the command of the Drina Corps. It is marked "strictly confidential." The date is the 13th of July, 1995. And it is an order which refers to the search of terrain. It is an order, therefore. Then we have the names of the brigades to which the order is issued. And further down in the text, it says what is actually being ordered. "I hereby order..." And the commander, as far as I can see, was General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And under point 1, although it's a very poor copy, but he says: "I hereby order, one, to the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade shall search the terrain" and then it goes on to state which areas the search should be conducted in. That would roughly be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I could show you what has been marked as D18/1 for identification purposes. Just take a look at it. That's dated 14 July 1995. If you could look at it, please, and when you...

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've taken a look at it, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could look at the bottom of the page, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is "Commander, Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's the same signature that's also on the earlier order, is it not, on the July 5, 1995, same stamp, same signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the question, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was waiting for the answer.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't asked me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question was, the signature that's at the bottom of the page on the order of the 14th, is it not the same signature as the order on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're now forcing me to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Don't guess.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to analyse the signatures. As far as I remember, as far as I remember, the signature is similar. As to the stamp, I can't really see it properly, what it says. But there is a stamp, and there is a signature, and it says: "Vidoje Blagojevic" which means -- I assume this is his signature, plus this stamp on this document. Now, I'm not an expert witness to be able to identify actual signatures and stamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you look at the order itself of 14 July 1995, can we assume or conclude that the order that was prepared by your commander on the 14th July 1995 was based on the order that he had received from his commander on the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, one could say that this order by the brigade commander from the Bratunac Brigade dated the 14th of July, we could say that it was based, it was founded on the order from the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's be a little more precise. The order from the Drina Corps, as you will see on the -- the top left portion, it says: "Strictly confidential, number 01/4-157/5." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we go now to the other document dated July 14th, which is D18/1 for identification, it says on the first line: "On the basis of strictly confidential order number 01/4-157/5." Are the numbers not the same?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Karnavas -- it is correct, Mr. Karnavas, that Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic, the brigade commander, is referring to the order of the Drina Corps command, and the number it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the Drina Corps has ordered your commander to search the terrain, to search a particular area of terrain. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you look at your commander's order, in fact, he does task the 1st infantry battalion, the 2nd infantry battalion, the 3rd, and the 4th, does he not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what the order says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it when you look at this order, paragraph 1, there are some numbers and some letters and some trig points, I take it those are references that one would find on a map, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Most of these places can be found on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it Momir Nikolic, chief of intelligence and security, would be able to find these points on the map, would he not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the necessary time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the task has a particular completion date, does it not, or an anticipated completion point, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That completion date is 16 July 1995? Well, let me rephrase. There are two dates, 16 July and 17 July 1995. The search is to be completed by 16 July 1995, under paragraph 5, or at least that's what it appears to say. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The starting point, this was issued on the 14th, they were to commence immediately. Is that correct? Under point 5, search will --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "They were to commence immediately and complete by the 16th of July 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That they would commence immediately and complete it by the 16th. And then it has another date, the 17th, and that's when they would have to report to their commander, your commander, that the task had indeed been completed pursuant to his order dated 14 July 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, it's all here in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know it's here in the order. I want you to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is inappropriate for him just to match and mix. There's no point to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, you have to ask a question to this witness, whether he received this order or not, whether he knew of this order at that time, or along this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this order before when you were working as the chief of intelligence and security of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive this order, and it was never addressed to me personally, at least as far as I can remember. I don't see anywhere in this order that I was involved or the police platoon. I don't see why there would have been a reason for this to be sent to the chief of the organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware as the chief of intelligence and security that an order had been issued by your commander for the various battalions to search the terrain pursuant to an order that had been issued by the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer the first part of your question first. I was aware of the fact that brigade units, that is, battalions, were engaged in searching the terrain throughout this period. I did not know at that time, however, pursuant to which order, nor was I familiar with the content of the order written by the commander and everything it says here. The way this reads, these orders were sent directly to units participating in the search. I knew about the units engaged in the -- in searching the terrain. I did not pursuant to which specific order the commander had issued this order. And I did not see this order prior to coming here and receiving it as part of the package of documents that the Office of the Prosecutor has provided me with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any doubts as to the authenticity of this order that was provided to us by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubts about any of the documents presented by your side or the Prosecution. I don't even wish to comment on that. All I can do is offer my opinions. All I can do is answer questions, whether I received something or not. But I can't be made to act as an expert here. I'm not here to judge the authenticity of any documents. It's simply not my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's switch to another topic. You were asked a question by the Prosecution whether there was a separate chain of command. Do you recall being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the question the Prosecutor asked towards the end of examination-in-chief, whether at one point there had been a takeover or disturbance in the chain of command of the Bratunac Brigade. If I remember correctly, that was the question in relation to a dispatch, if I remember correctly, from the main staff about the appointment of three officers, if I remember correctly. And I tried to answer that question. What I said was that there was no disturbance to the chain of command in the Bratunac Brigade. That's what I said, if that's what your question was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you ever have to go around your own commander and report directly to Popovic, Kosoric, or Beara, or whatever else you thought you might need to report to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had a need to go around any commander. I'm not speaking only ever Commander Blagojevic. I never had a need to go around any commander as for reporting on matters that were within my purview of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So your answer is that you didn't have a need. My question did you ever do it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't go around anyone. Whatever was defined as my task, my responsibility, my duty from either of the areas that I was in charge of, I never felt the need to go around any of the commanders in terms of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Under the rules -- well, let me ask you this: Have you ever heard the term "counterintelligence"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you are engaged -- have you ever engaged in any activities that could be characterised as counterintelligence? I'm not asking for specifics, but if you could just tell us in general yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, counterintelligence activity and counterintelligence assessment means the uncovering, monitoring, and prevention of activity carried out by elements or intelligence services of the enemy against your unit, your command, your institution, individuals from your units or buildings in which weaponry and equipment is stored. This is common knowledge. Everything that concerns counterintelligence activity and work or taking measures, taking counterintelligence measures, including the drawing up of a counterintelligence assessment, all of this is done by the organ within the unit. I was constantly making these assessments. I was constantly monitoring the activity of all those that I believed could have a detrimental effect on my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the answer to my question is yes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in this context that I was talking about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were engaged in counterintelligence, in your position as the chief of the security organ, are you required at all times to inform your commander of your activities, or can you bypass your commander, conduct your activities, and report to a superior command through a separate chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, there is no need for me to report to a superior command through bypassing my own commander. These assessments, the assessment of a potential threat or a potential enemy, group or individual, I would file this away myself because this would pose an immediate threat to my brigade, not to the corps command. We're talking about the security and safety of my units. Why would I need to report this to the corps command and bypass my own commander at the same time? I assure you, there would have been no need for me to report this to the corps command simply because an issue like this would have been of interest first and foremost to the safety and security of my own unit. This is a perfectly legal and usual task for a security organ. It includes no secrets whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you ever issued orders from your superior command to conduct counterintelligence activity? I'm not talking about gathering information now. You're receiving an order, say, from Popovic or Beara for you to conduct what would be characterised or what you would assess to be counterintelligence activity.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such orders that I received from Popovic or anyone else in relation to anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it from your testimony, maybe I have it wrong, but I was under the impression that all the mail that comes in to the Bratunac Brigade, even when directed to the security organ, it's read by the commander before it gets to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I never said anything quite like that. What I said is that all mail arriving in the form of orders, instructions, announcements would be coded, received through the communications centre in a coded form. These were daily telexes that would go to the communications centre. After that, after that, there were regulations describing how and to whom this mail should then be sent. The regulation prescribes that all mail reaching the Bratunac Brigade command should be sent to the commander directly and personally, and then he may, if he pleases, go through it, see who the document is addressed to, and then the mail would be distributed throughout the brigade. Or the commander may choose to authorise someone else in the command, the chief of staff, or the chief of operations and training to go through the mail and set aside whatever they believed was of interest. The commander may decide to entrust someone with this task, an officer from the brigade command. Any officer might go to the communications centre and tell the man working there, having received a telex for the security and intelligence organ, they would tell them: "Take this straight to Nikolic, leave it on his table." Or the assistant commander for logistics, for example, the commander could always make certain aberrations from the usual regulations concerning the incoming mail and the distribution of this mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did the commander of the Bratunac Brigade open your mail, mail that was addressed to you as head of the security?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I said this, with the possible exception of one single case, and it has been a long time so I hope I remember this correctly, there was no need for me to receive my mail in an envelope. While Colonel Blagojevic was there, as far as I can remember, I received no mail whatsoever in envelopes. Those were the usual channels. While the previous commander was there, I'm talking about Commander Ognjenovic, there was one such case where I informed the corps command about a suspicion I had that certain crimes had been committed by Commander Ognjenovic, and then I received from the command --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Object. That was a specific answer to a specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness finish first, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record, it's not responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We can only judge that after we hear what the witness is going to tell us. You may continue, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Karnavas, it only happened once that I needed to use this method, as I said in my testimony, when there was -- there were grounds to suspect that the brigade commander had committed a criminal offence or that he was involved in some form of criminal activity. And if you received authorisation from the corps command to continue to gather intelligence concerning these crimes, then this mail coming and going then the mutual reports between you and the superior command -- between me and the superior command in this case would travel in sealed envelopes addressed to the chief of security of the Drina Corps, and no one opened this mail. The consequence of my work, of my work on this specific case was that the brigade commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic, following an investigation by the main staff was removed from his post. It was proven that my suspicion had been well founded, my suspicion about him having committed a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, listen to the question: Did the brigade commander have the right to open your mail? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commander did not have the authority to open my mail, mail that was addressed to me, sealed across, addressed personally to Momir Nikolic, chief of intelligence and security. As for all the rest, as for normal, everyday mail, it wasn't even closed. So Commander Blagojevic had -- would have an opportunity to familiarise himself with everything else that was addressed the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you required to show your commander - and I'm not talking about Colonel Blagojevic, any commander - were you required to share all of your reports with your commander, your immediate commander, before sending them off to Beara or Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, as for my regular daily reports, usually the commanders at my brigade didn't insist on these reports being brought to them personally for them to review them. What I know is that the commanders I worked with had sufficient confidence in my work. They were always fully informed about my reports to the superior command whenever security and intelligence information was involved, or anything else for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So my question was were you required to show your commander your reports before sending them up to the Drina Corps security, or even further higher? Were you required at all times? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, under the law, my obligation was to show the commander the report, but this was not the established practice because the commanders did not insist on me showing them my reports. They didn't always request that, not all the commanders were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. Did all of the information that you passed on to your superior commanders in the security organ, did you pass all of that information to your commander or commanders, since you went through quite a few of them, at all times prior to sending that information either orally or in a report to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, again, you've asked me countless questions like this. As a rule, or rather, almost never, you never forwarded oral reports to the corps commander or the superior command. If you write up a report, then that's a written report to the corps command. So that was your first question, if I remember. The next question, you asked if I got it right whether I informed both the commander and the corps command about all the information I received. If the commander requests to review a report that I'm sending in writing, it means that the commander gets an opportunity to see what I write and what I sign. That's, I believe, what you asked me. Now, as for selective reports, now for the commander and now for the Drina Corps, there were no such things. I'd report on the day's activity to the commander and throughout the evening. That was the usual way to perform these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So based on your answer, if your commander wished to see your report, he would have to ask you to share that report -- for you to share that report with him before you send it up to the Drina Corps. That's your answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Karnavas. That's your answer. My answer, Mr. Karnavas, is the following: The commander has no reason to request anything from me; rather, he gives me an order and he says: "Captain Nikolic, as of today, before you send another report to the Drina Corps, every report you send must be brought and left on my table first. That's on order." If he tells me: "Captain Nikolic, you are free to send on security reports to the Drina Corps command" and then two or three days later, whenever there's a briefing, then you inform me" then that's what I do. What I do depends on the commander. Not on me. I know there's a rule it's my obligation to inform the commander about everything, but as for the mode or rather the method as to how I was to inform him, that was something decided by the commander, not by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an instruction that was drafted, signed -- make sure I got the title right- "Commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic" dated October 24th, 1994, with respect to the management and command of security intelligence agencies of the Republika Srpska army. Are you familiar with that instruction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If specific documents are going to be referenced, if we could see that or have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to be getting it. I was just merely asking the question if he had ever heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Obviously we're going to be providing it to him and to Mr. McCloskey from whom we received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, just to clarify the record, this doesn't have any ERN numbers on it. And we'll work with Mr. Karnavas to figure out where it came from. But it's not a document that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he were to look at the original version, Mr. McCloskey's not familiar with it because obviously he didn't read the document because it's in Serbian and to be translated. This is our translation. But we received this, and I believe the document has some numbers on it, DAO1-0961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, it's very late and everybody's tired. Are you going to proceed on this document? Or we stop here? It depends on you. How long are you going to use for this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think this document is going to take some time, Your Honour. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So could we break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I just wanted to, like, get it in. But I think this would be a very good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just wanted to clear up, this number that Mr. Karnavas has referred to is not an ERN number but it is a number that we do recognise from one of your collections. So he has helped us out on that reference, and we'll be able to find it, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're not playing any games, Your Honour. We're just doing our best, doing our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, shall we resume next Monday morning, 9.00 in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, the hearing is adjourned.
